Subject: Sizing ask: Helm Systems inference profile and headroom

Hi Jordan —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Per our internal planning conversation, Helm Systems is aiming to sign a reserved capacity commitment for conversational + retrieval-augmented assistant workloads. Before we lock numbers with procurement we need a clear mapping from our expected request profile to Redwood Dedicated slabs (GPU count + expected p95 gen latency), including recommended safety buffer.

Quick snapshot of our workload (requested):
- Peak active sessions: 1,100 users (peak region: US-West)
- Average interactive cadence: ~6 requests/user/hour during peak; heavy users up to 20/hr
- Median prompt size: 160 input tokens, median generation: 240 tokens (avg total tokens per request ~400)
- Some flows (batch summarization) produce 1K-2K output tokens but are infrequent (~3% of requests)
- SLA target: p95 end-to-end generation latency <= 700ms for interactive flows; tail tolerance up to 1.2s on rare spikes

Two asks for Redwood:
1) A tokens/sec steady-state and peak tokens/sec estimate mapped to an explicit GPU count and recommended slab commit for a 12-month contract.
2) Explain headroom assumptions (batching, KV caching, cold-starts, autoscale burst lanes) and the conservative multiplier you recommend for the initial commit.

I attached our crude workload export (helm_workload_model.xlsx). Can someone on your sizing team take this and return a simple capacity tiling proposal we can include in procurement?

Cheers,
Alex
Head of Platform, Helm Systems

Subject: Helm Systems — capacity tiling proposal (draft)

Team / Alex — draft sizing below. I pulled Helm's sheet and made the following high-level assumptions (callouts first):
- Model mix: primary generation on 13B-quant variant (open 13B int4-style) with a smaller fraction (~8%) of 70B-class reranks for enterprise workflows; recommendation is to serve the 70B workloads on on-demand Dedicated burst lanes to avoid permanent slab allocation.
- Runtime optimizations: continuous batching, KV prefix cache with an assumed hit rate of 72% (Helm indicated many repeated prompts), and kernel selection tuned for sequence lengths <= 512 for interactive flows.
- Serving HW baseline: A100-80GB equivalency per slab GPU (we'll convert to your preferred cloud SKU later). Throughput numbers below use our internal A100-baseline profiling.

Workload translation (summary):
- Median tokens/request: 400
- Estimated interactive peak qps (requests/sec) from Helm export: 220 RPS (US-West peak)
- Peak tokens/sec (unthrottled) = 220 RPS * 400 tokens = 88,000 tokens/sec

Effective tokens/sec after KV cache hit-rate and prompt templating: assume 72% KV-hit and 18% token reduction from templating for cached flows. Effective tokens/sec ~= 88,000 * (1 - 0.72) * (1 - 0.18) + 88,000 * 0.72 * (1 - 0.18) * 0.12  // we model partial reuse for illustrative purposes — simplifies to ~32,000 tokens/sec aggregate demand.

Per-GPU capability (empirical):
- 13B-quant (continuous batching): steady sustained gen throughput ~1,800 tokens/sec per A100-equivalent GPU at p95 latency <= 650ms under mixed-request sizes.
- Short-burst envelope (autoscale / burst lanes): a single GPU with aggressive batching can spike to ~3,000 tokens/sec but with degraded p95 to ~1.1s for worst-case long generations.

Sizing recommendation (committed slab):
- Steady allocation: 18 x A100-equivalent GPUs -> capacity ~32,400 tokens/sec (18 * 1,800). This matches modeled effective tokens/sec with ~1.0125x headroom for steady-state.
- Burst/Autoscale policy: reserve 6 GPUs as instant-burst pool available for <10-minute events (on a credit/committed-burst plan) to cover multi-region peaks and the 3% long-run batches. Burst pool provides up to additional ~10,800 tokens/sec transient capacity.
- Safety buffer logic: we recommend contractual headroom of 1.5x on the committed slab for the first 3 months to allow traffic-pattern tuning and prompt engineering. Practically that means starting with 18 committed GPUs but with option to convert 3 burst GPUs into committed if usage stabilizes higher.

Latency mapping: at 32k tokens/sec aggregate demand mapped to 18 GPUs:
- Expected p95 token-latency for median interactive flows (<=512 tokens): ~520-650ms end-to-end (includes RPC overhead + first-token generation).
- p99 tail during bursts without additional autoscale: could reach ~1.0-1.4s for some long-generation requests; adding the burst pool keeps p95 below 700ms for the traffic mix described.

Operational notes & tradeoffs:
- KV cache priming: warm the common prefixes during ramp windows; we observed 12-18% effective token savings after a 24-hour warm-up for similar customers.
- Quantization: if Helm is comfortable with int4 execution for selected flows we can improve per-GPU tokens/sec by ~25%, reducing the slab by ~4 GPUs for steady-state. This is a recommended ops experiment after go-live.
- Quiet-hour smoothing: shift non-interactive heavy jobs (the 3% long summaries) to scheduled off-peak windows to flatten peaks and reduce burst consumption.

Deliverables attached: helm_workload_model_sizing_tab.xlsx (I exported a worksheet with the above math) and a short PDF note (redwood_capacity_notes.pdf).

Next steps: Jordan/Alex, if you want this packaged into a procurement-ready commitment we can draft the commitment table with monthly expected token allocations, burst credit terms, and an on-call ops runbook for on-prem KV support.

Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Ben / Jordan / Alex — quick clarify and a runtime suggestion before we hand this to procurement.

Clarifications on Ben's assumptions (so procurement can read plainly):
1) The per-GPU 1,800 tps number assumes continuous batching at batch windows of 8-12 for interactive traffic and a KV-cache hit-rate of 72%. If Helm sees lower cache reuse (e.g., 40-50%), effective per-GPU throughput will drop ~30% and you'll need ~6 additional GPUs under the same headroom policy.

2) The 18-GPU slab is our conservative steadystate mapping with 1.0x mapping to the modeled effective tokens/sec; the recommended contractual buffer of 1.5x is expressed as an ops/scale policy rather than immediate hardware — it allows us to keep commitment lower while enabling fast conversion of burst lanes to committed if needed.

Runtime suggestion (proactive throttle / tiling):
- Implement a lightweight token-throttle layer at the edge that enforces per-session QPS and enqueues bulk summarization jobs into scheduled windows. This reduces peak simultaneous token pressure and improves cache hit-rate via more predictable prefixes. We can include a short SDK snippet as part of the onboarding docs.

If Alex approves, we'll format Ben's numbers into a one-page commitment table (GPU count, expected monthly token allocation, burst credits, SLA p95 target and escalation path) and send it over to procurement. Also propose a 30-day post-go-live review to potentially 1) enable int4 across non-sensitive flows, and 2) convert 3 burst GPUs to committed if observed steady usage exceeds modeled headroom.

Karthik Iyer
Senior Engineering Manager, Inference Runtime
